# Data Frames

## Tidy Data {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- There are many ways to store data

::: {.fragment .mt1}
- We will be learning the [tidy data]{.b .blue} format
    - Data should be *rectangular*
    - Each [variable]{.green} has its own column
    - Each [observation]{.green} has its own row
    - Each [value]{.green} has its own cell
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
![](../../img/tidydata.png)
:::

:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/spreadsheet.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

## Other Data Advice {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Name all variables]{.b .blue} in the first row
    -   This is called a [header row]{.b .green}
    
::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [Avoid merged cells]{.b .blue} for data storage
    -   These are okay for communication
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [Avoid empty cells]{.b .blue} whenever possible
    -   Mark [missing data]{.b .green} as `NA`
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [Avoid formatting-as-data]{.b .blue} for storage
    -   e.g., non-redundant color-coding
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/light_bulb.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

## Tibbles {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   R works particularly well with [tidy data]{.b .green}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   We store tidy data in [data frames]{.b .green} or [tibbles]{.b .blue}
    -   Tibbles are just fancier data frames<br />
        (i.e., they have a few extra features)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   To use tibbles, we need the [tidyverse]{.b .blue} package
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Tibbles are constructed from one or more vectors
    -   The vectors must have the [same length]{.b .green}
    -   They can contain [different types]{.b .green} of data
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/new_train.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::


## Parallel Vectors {.fs70}

![](../../img/vectors.png)

::: {.tc .pv4}
We start with three separate vector objects that all have the same length.

We set it up so that the $n$-th car in each train corresponds to the same observation.
:::


## Tibble {.fs70}

![](../../img/tibble.png)

::: {.tc .pv4}
Then we combine the vectors into a single tibble (or data frame) object.

Now, as the tibble moves around, the variables always stay together.
:::


## Loading the tidyverse

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Install it once via [Extras pane > Packages tab > Install]{.b .blue}, then load it
each session. One `library()` call brings in the whole collection --- readr,
dplyr, ggplot2 and the rest --- so this is the only line most scripts need.
:::

## Creating a Tibble from Vectors

```{r}
#| echo: true

x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)

y <- x * 2 - 4
y

my_tibble <- tibble(x, y)
my_tibble
```

::: {.takeaway}
`tibble()` lines vectors up as columns, using each vector's name as the column
name. They must be the same length --- these are rows of one dataset.
:::

## Tibbles Can Mix Types

```{r}
#| echo: true

first_names <- c("Adam", "Billy", "Caitlyn", "Debra")

age_years <- c(12, 13, 10, NA)

guests <- tibble(first_names, age_years)
guests
```

::: {.takeaway}
Look at the `<chr>` and `<dbl>` labels --- a tibble tracks each column's type, and
prints `NA` where a value is missing rather than guessing at one.
:::

## Building the Vectors Inline

```{r}
#| echo: true

gradebook <- tibble(
  grade = c(95, 83, 90, 76),
  letter = c("a", "b", "a-", "c")
)
gradebook
```

::: {.takeaway}
Naming the columns inside `tibble()` skips the separate vectors entirely --- less
to type, and nothing left lying around afterwards.
:::

## Pitfall: Unequal Column Lengths

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true

tibble(y = c(1, 2, 3), x = c("a", "b"))
```

::: {.takeaway}
Every column is one variable measured on the same rows, so they must all be the
same length. R does make one exception: a column of length 1 is repeated down the
whole tibble.
:::

## Extracting a Column with $

```{r}
#| echo: true

mytibble <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), y = "test")

mytibble$x

mytibble$y
```

::: {.takeaway}
`$` pulls one column out as a plain vector. Note `y`: a single value is recycled
down the whole column --- length one is the one length allowed to differ.
:::

## Pitfall: A Column That Does Not Exist

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: true

mytibble$z
```

::: {.takeaway}
This is [not]{.b} an error. You get `NULL` and a warning, so a typo in a column
name can **flow silently** into the rest of your code.
:::

## Getting Information About a Tibble

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Rows and columns
dim(gradebook)

# Column names
colnames(gradebook)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Worth running on any dataset you did not build yourself, before you write code
that assumes what is in it.
:::

## Data Files {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   Data is usually stored in [data files]{.b .green}
    -   Importing files into R is called [reading]{.b .blue}
    -   Exporting files from R is called [writing]{.b .blue}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   A convenient data file type is a CSV
    -   This stands for [comma-separated values]{.b .green}
    -   A CSV file is easy to share with other people
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   The [tidyverse]{.b .green} package can read/write CSVs
    -   Other packages can read/write other types
        (e.g., *readxl*, *haven*, *rio*, *googlesheets4*)
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/freight_ship.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::


## Getting a Data File {.fs70}

-   Download [`gradebook.csv`]{.b .blue} from the course website into your project folder

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   You can see it in the [Extras pane > Files tab]{.b .green}
    -   And open it in another program, such as Excel
:::

## Reading in a Data File

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]

old_gradebook <- read_csv("../../data/gradebook.csv")
old_gradebook
```

::: {.takeaway}
`read_csv()` examines each column and guesses its type. You can state the types
yourself, but the guess is usually right --- check it rather than assume it.
:::

## Pitfall: Missing Values in Disguise

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]

old_gradebook <- read_csv("../../data/gradebook.csv", na = "?")
old_gradebook
```

::: {.takeaway}
One grade was recorded as `?`. R has no way to know that means "missing" --- until
you say so with `na = "?"` it stays a real value, and the whole column is read as
text rather than numbers.
:::

## Other Kinds of Data File {.fs70}

-   [readxl]{.b .blue} and [googlesheets4]{.b .blue} --- spreadsheets

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [haven]{.b .blue} --- files from SPSS, SAS, and STATA
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [rio]{.b .blue} --- tries to detect the type and read in anything
:::


# Data Exploration

## Data Verification {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   It's always a good idea to start with [verification]{.b .blue}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Check that your variables are the [correct type]{.b .green}
    -   Configure your [factors]{.b .green}' levels and labels
    -   Establish ordinal factors' ordering
    -   Explicitly set your [missing values]{.b .green} to NA
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Check variables' [extrema]{.b .green} and [distributions]{.b .green}
    -   Check for erroneous and outlying values
    -   Check the shape of continuous distributions
    -   Check the overlap of categorical levels
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/avatar_search.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

## Reading in the Raw Penguins Data

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(easystats)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]

penguins <- read_csv("../../data/penguins0.csv")
penguins
```

::: {.takeaway}
`species`, `island`, and `sex` arrived as numbers, not categories.
:::

## Configuring the Factors

```{r}
#| echo: true

penguins$species <- factor(penguins$species, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                           labels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))

penguins$island <- factor(penguins$island, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                          labels = c("Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen"))

penguins$sex <- factor(penguins$sex, levels = c(1, 2),
                       labels = c("female", "male"))
```

::: {.takeaway}
The same `factor()` call as before, applied one column at a time with `$`. Tedious
but explicit --- and exactly the work a cleaning script exists to hold.
:::

## The Configured Data

```{r}
#| echo: true

penguins
```

::: {.takeaway}
Those three columns now print as `<fct>` with readable values. Save the cleaned
version with `write_csv()` so this is done **once**, not every session.
:::

## Checking the Summary for Problems

```{r}
#| echo: true

summary(penguins)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Read the `NA` counts: 2 penguins were never measured and 11 (including those 2)
were never sexed. Real data has holes, and this is where you find them.
:::

## Describing One Continuous Variable

```{r}
#| echo: true

describe_distribution(penguins, body_mass)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Mean, SD, range, and the count of missing values in one line --- the numbers you
would otherwise ask for one function at a time.
:::

## Describing All of Them at Once

```{r}
#| echo: true

describe_distribution(penguins)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Name no column and it describes every continuous one, skipping the factors. A good
first look at a dataset you have just read in.
:::

## Tabulating One Factor

```{r}
#| echo: true

data_tabulate(penguins, species)
```

::: {.takeaway}
The factor counterpart of `describe_distribution()`: counts and percentages, with
missing values shown rather than dropped.
:::

## Tabulating Every Factor

```{r}
#| echo: true

data_tabulate(penguins, is.factor)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Passing `is.factor` tabulates every factor at once --- the categorical half of the
same first look.
:::

## Data Visualization {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Variable distributions]{.b .blue} are critical in data analysis
    -   What are the most and least [common values]{.b .green}?
    -   What are the [extrema]{.b .green} (min and max values)?
    -   Are there any [outliers]{.b .green} or impossible values?
    -   How much [spread]{.b .green} is there in the variable?
    -   What [shape]{.b .green} does the distribution take?

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Distributions describe a single variable's [variation]{.b .green}
    -   We also visualize many variables' [covariation]{.b .blue}
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/dice.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

## Loading the Cleaned Data

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]

penguins <- read_csv("../../data/penguins.csv")
```

::: {.takeaway}
This is the tidied version of the file we just walked through --- factors
configured, missing values read correctly. Everything that follows uses it, and
you will meet it again in later chapters.
:::

## Variation of a Factor

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| warning: true

qplot(x = species, data = penguins, geom = "bar")
```

::: aside
*Note.* `qplot()` warns that it is deprecated. It still works and we will keep using it here; the warning appears once per session, not once per plot.
:::

## Variation of Another Factor

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = island, data = penguins, geom = "bar")
```

## Variation of a Continuous Variable

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = flipper_len, data = penguins, geom = "histogram")
```

## The Same Variable as a Boxplot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = flipper_len, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot")
```

## Body Mass as a Histogram

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "histogram")
```

## Body Mass as a Boxplot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot")
```

## Two Continuous Variables

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "point")
```

## Covariation of Two Factors

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = species, y = island, data = penguins, geom = "jitter")
```

## The Same Pair as Stacked Bars

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = species, fill = island, data = penguins, geom = "bar")
```

## A Factor and a Continuous Variable

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = body_mass, y = species, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot")
```

## The Same Pair as Violins

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

qplot(x = body_mass, y = species, data = penguins, geom = "violin")
```
